1.title: The Burden of the Word
1.context: Malachi means 'my messenger,' and some readers take it as a title rather than a personal name. The book is usually dated to the mid-400s BC, after the temple was rebuilt and around the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.
1.question: When has God's love been hard for you to see in your circumstances?

1.title: Jacob and Esau
1.context: Paul quotes these words in Romans 9:13. Christians read them differently: some see God's choice of individuals, others see God's choosing of nations, and many note that 'hated' can be a Hebrew way of saying 'not chosen' or 'loved less' (compare Genesis 29:30–31).
1.question: How do you respond when God's ways of choosing are hard to understand?

1.title: They May Build
1.context: Edom lay south and east of the Dead Sea. By Malachi's time, Arab peoples were pushing the Edomites out of their land, and Obadiah had earlier announced judgment on Edom for its treatment of Judah.
1.question: Where are you tempted to rebuild something God has asked you to let go?

1.title: Beyond the Borders of Israel
1.context: Malachi repeatedly looks to God's greatness among the nations (Malachi 1:11, 1:14). The phrase can be read as 'over the border of Israel,' meaning God's care for His people, or 'beyond' it, meaning His rule over the whole world.
1.question: Where have you seen God's faithfulness with your own eyes?

1.title: The Pattern of the Book
1.context: Malachi is built as a series of disputes: God makes a statement, the people object with a question, and God answers. The same pattern runs through all six episodes.
1.question: What questions do you find yourself bringing back to God?

2.title: A Son Honors His Father
2.context: Priests were descendants of Aaron from the tribe of Levi, responsible for sacrifices and for teaching God's law. The LORD of Hosts, a title meaning the LORD of heaven's armies, appears more than twenty times in Malachi.
2.question: What does honoring God look like in the ordinary routines of your week?

2.title: Try Offering Them to Your Governor
2.context: The law required sacrificial animals without defect (Leviticus 22:20–22; Deuteronomy 15:21). Judah was a province of the Persian Empire, ruled by a governor.
2.question: Is there anywhere you give God what is left over rather than your best?

2.title: Shut the Temple Doors
2.context: Readers understand verse 11 in different ways: some see a prophecy of worship among the nations in the future, others see God honoring sincere worship already offered beyond Israel. Either way, the passage widens God's name to the whole world.
2.question: How might God be calling you to worship from the heart rather than out of habit?

2.title: What a Nuisance!
2.context: A vow was a voluntary promise to give God an offering (Leviticus 27). Making a vow and then substituting a lesser animal turned a free gift into a deception.
2.question: When has worship started to feel like a burden to you, and what might renew it?

2.title: The Covenant of Levi
2.context: The covenant with Levi recalls Numbers 25:10–13 and Deuteronomy 33:8–10, where the Levites are given the work of priesthood and teaching. Malachi stresses the priest's role as a teacher of true instruction.
2.question: Who has been a trustworthy teacher of God's word in your life?

3.title: One Father
3.context: Readers differ on whether 'one Father' refers to God as Creator or to an ancestor such as Abraham or Jacob. The Hebrew word for 'break faith' appears five times in Malachi 2:10–16.
3.question: Where is God calling you to keep faith with someone today?

3.title: The Daughter of a Foreign God
3.context: Ezra 9–10 and Nehemiah 13:23–27 describe the same problem of marriage to those who worshiped other gods in this period. The concern in the text is faithfulness to the LORD, not ethnicity.
3.question: What competes for your loyalty to God in your closest relationships?

3.title: Tears on the Altar
3.context: The text does not say whose tears cover the altar. Some readers see the worshipers' own weeping when God rejects their offerings, others the grief of wives who were sent away.
3.question: Is there any grief around you that you have been slow to notice?

3.title: The LORD Is Witness
3.context: Verse 15 is one of the hardest verses in the Old Testament to translate, and versions differ widely. Its clear points are that God made husband and wife one and that He seeks godly offspring.
3.question: What does it mean to you that God is a witness to the promises you make?

3.title: Do Not Break Faith
3.context: Translations of verse 16 differ: some read 'I hate divorce' as God's words, while others read that a man who hates and divorces his wife covers his garment with violence. Christians hold a range of views on divorce, but all readings condemn treating a spouse with cruelty.
3.question: How can you guard your spirit and keep faith with the people closest to you?

4.title: Where Is the God of Justice?
4.context: The same complaint about the wicked prospering appears in Psalm 73 and Habakkuk 1. Malachi records it as the people's words, not as the book's own view.
4.question: When have you been tempted to think that God does not see injustice?

4.title: Behold, I Will Send My Messenger
4.context: The Gospels apply the first part of this verse to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus (Matthew 11:10; Mark 1:2). Interpreters discuss whether 'the Messenger of the covenant' is the same figure as the Lord who comes to His temple.
4.question: What would it look like for you to prepare the way for God in your life?

4.title: A Refiner's Fire
4.context: A refiner heated silver until impurities rose to the surface and could be removed. A launderer, or fuller, cleaned cloth with strong lye soap.
4.question: What might God be refining in you through a difficult season?

4.title: A Swift Witness
4.context: The law repeatedly commands care for widows, orphans, foreigners and hired workers (Deuteronomy 24:14–22). Malachi links true worship with justice toward the vulnerable.
4.question: Who around you is vulnerable, and how could you stand with them?

4.title: I Do Not Change
4.context: God's unchanging nature is also affirmed in Numbers 23:19 and James 1:17. Here it is the reason Israel survives despite its unfaithfulness.
4.question: How does God's faithfulness give you hope when you have not been faithful?

5.title: Return to Me
5.context: The call 'Return to Me, and I will return to you' repeats Zechariah 1:3 almost word for word. Joel 2:12 calls the people to return in a similar way.
5.question: What would one concrete step of return look like for you this week?

5.title: Will a Man Rob God?
5.context: The tithe was a tenth of produce and livestock, used to support the Levites, the priests, and the poor (Numbers 18:21–24; Deuteronomy 14:28–29). Nehemiah 13:10–12 describes the Levites leaving the temple because the tithes had not been brought.
5.question: Where might you be holding back from God what is rightly His?

5.title: Test Me in This
5.context: The storehouse was a set of rooms at the temple where tithes of grain, wine and oil were kept. Christians differ on whether the tithe is required today or whether the New Testament calls for generous, cheerful giving without a fixed amount (2 Corinthians 9:6–7).
5.question: What would it mean for you to trust God with your giving?

5.title: I Will Rebuke the Devourer
5.context: The devourer is usually understood as locusts or other crop pests, the kind of plague Joel 1 describes.
5.question: What 'devourer' do you need God to rebuke in your life?

5.title: A Land of Delight
5.context: God's blessing of Israel among the nations recalls His promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:2–3).
5.question: How might your life show others the goodness of God?

6.title: It Is Futile to Serve God
6.context: Psalm 73 voices the same complaint that the wicked seem to prosper while the faithful suffer, before the psalmist sees things differently in God's presence.
6.question: When have you wondered whether following God is worth it?

6.title: A Scroll of Remembrance
6.context: Ancient Persian kings kept records of those who served them (Esther 6:1–3). The Bible also speaks of God's book in Exodus 32:32, Psalm 69:28 and Daniel 12:1.
6.question: Who could you speak with this week to encourage each other in faith?

6.title: My Treasured Possession
6.context: 'Treasured possession' echoes Exodus 19:5, where God calls Israel His own special possession at Sinai.
6.question: What does it mean to you to be God's treasured possession?

6.title: The Sun of Righteousness
6.context: In Hebrew Bibles these verses are Malachi 3:19–21; English Bibles number them as chapter 4. 'Wings' may picture the rays of the rising sun. Many Christians have read the sun of righteousness as a picture of Christ.
6.question: Where do you need the healing of the sun of righteousness?

6.title: Elijah the Prophet
6.context: In Hebrew Bibles these verses are Malachi 3:22–24. The Gospels connect this promise with John the Baptist (Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14; 17:10–13). In Christian Bibles these are the last words of the Old Testament.
6.question: Whose heart is God calling you to turn toward in your own family?
